text: Beyond selling live animals, smallholders may sell milk, eggs, chicks, and breeding animals, but the importance of each depends on the farming system. Village chicken production is widespread (Cambodian research found over 80% of smallholders keep local breeds), making eggs and live poultry the more realistic recurring smallholder products. Dairy cattle production is more specialized -- do not assume dairy is a normal income activity for every Preah Vihear smallholder without farmer-specific confirmation. For farmers who do sell milk (ទឹកដោះគោ), it is highly perishable and supports rapid microbial growth, so hygiene (clean hands, containers, udders), rapid delivery, and cooling where actually available are critical; visual freshness does NOT guarantee safety, and brucellosis can transmit through infected milk, so pasteurization matters where relevant -- do not assume every farmer has refrigeration, and recommend delivering quickly rather than mandating a cold chain that may not exist. For eggs, protect from heat, moisture, breakage, and manure contamination, and collect regularly. A productive animal (laying hen, milking cow) has ongoing earning value -- compare one-time sale value against expected future product income minus feed/health costs before recommending a farmer sell it. Net income calculations should subtract feed, mortality, transport, breakage, rejected product, and labor from sales revenue, not just look at the selling price. During the wet season, rain complicates transport and hygiene for milk and eggs; during the dry season, heat accelerates spoilage of both. Do not invent a current milk or egg price, a specific dairy breed, or a specific Preah Vihear buyer/cooperative.
